message.content:
You are the cold reviewer for a decision brief (the stakeholder-presentation process's cold-read step), in a fresh context. Working directory: /home/vscode/rebaseline. Read basis/roles/cold-reviewer.md, basis/artifacts/decision-brief.md, basis/fitness/decision-brief.fitness.md, basis/guidelines/stakeholder-communication.md, then the brief under review: briefs/brief-032.md. Do NOT open the annex or any other file.

Read the presentation alone as the product authority — who has said reviewing every artifact and process type is getting in the way of the system working, and wants the whole process from discovery to assigned scenarios modeled and a plan to build it. Report stumbles in reading order with quotes; terms not introduced; per ask, decidability (confident / wobbly / cannot-decide) and whether binds vs drafting default are stated; an overload verdict; the decision-layer word count against ~400 and the whole against ~1500; the fitness scenarios; top three changes. Verdict "clean" only if nothing found; "tradeoffs-accepted" only if every remaining finding is marked in the text as accepted; otherwise "findings". Write to /tmp/claude-1000/-home-vscode-rebaseline/635ec80b-b74c-4200-8974-a7a6743a1e99/scratchpad/coldread-brief032-1.md and return it as your final message.

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Artifact type: decision-brief

## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `decision-brief`
- **Generic type:** request — it requests decisions.
  **Ancestry:** `request → decision-brief` (generic fallback: any validator
  that knows `request` may check this type at that level).
- **User-need quadrant:** action + work — the reader
  is deciding, now. One quadrant per document; a brief that drifts into
  explanation fails its type.
- **Produced by:** [`../processes/stakeholder-presentation.md`](../processes/stakeholder-presentation.md).
  **Consumed by:** the product authority, at a review.

## Required frontmatter

`type`, `id`, `status` (draft | delivered | decided), `version`,
`date`, `reader`, `decisions-requested` (count), `annex` (link).
Schema-validated; unknown keys rejected (closed field set, per the
authority's strictness directive). The cold-read round record lives as
`review` entries in the Document History — one per round with the
verdict and the judge's model — never in frontmatter, per the
definition typedef's Document History rule.

## Required sections

1. **The answer first** — SCQA opening, ≤4 sentences, then the
   recommendation; states which asks gate work and which default on silence.
2. **Asks** — each: question → recommendation → inline evidence → default.
   Block-approval asks state what approval binds vs what stays a
   drafting default.
3. **Deferred** (if anything is) — deferrals are notes, never asks.
4. **Annex link** — the full material, labeled optional.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A decision-brief is done when: the reader can make every requested decision
from the brief alone in one short reading; budgets hold (decision layer
≤ ~400 words, total ≤ ~1,500); an independent cold read has passed it (O3 of
the producing process). **Consequence on failure:** the brief returns to the
author for re-forming — it is not deliverable, and decisions made from a
failed brief are not recorded as approvals.

ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289 (generic content types); DITA-style ancestry
declaration; Scrum's artifact-commitment pairing; layer and ask structure
from Minto/SCQA, BLUF, and government briefing-note practice.

# Brief 032: the product flow from discovery to assigned scenarios

**The answer first.** The gap you see is real: discovery ends at a
session record, and nothing carries an idea from there to a scenario a
shop can take up. The annex models the whole path as one top-level
process, `product-flow`, composed of six sub-processes — three exist
(discovery, the PO output check, scenario assignment), two are new
(`initiative-check`, `feature-authoring`), one is new and small
(`backlog-ordering`). Building it is five batches, four screens, five
approvals as blocks, about five sessions at the current pace — then
Phase 2's first feature runs through it. Recommendation: approve the
model, the build order, and block approval per batch. Ask 1 gates the
work; asks 2 and 3 default on silence.

## Asks

**1. Approve the model.** *What you approve:* the flow in the annex —
discovery (brainstorm first) records an initiative as `proposed`;
`initiative-check` attaches feasibility, decomposition, and usability,
screens it, and puts the bet to you inside the check (`planned`,
stays `proposed`, or `cancelled`); the PO places it in the backlog
order, authors each feature with the owning shops, and the existing
check screens it; assignment tags and dispatches its scenarios; the
loop runs until every feature is assigned. *Binds:* the six
sub-processes and their hand-offs. *Drafting default:* step wording,
prompts, and caps. *Evidence:* every hop the system read found
undefined is now a named step; the bet moves inside the check, which
removes one pending process amendment. *Default:* none — gates the
build.

**2. Approve the build order and block approval.** *What you
approve:* batches A–E in the annex, each screened once as a set and
approved as a block, rather than per definition per round.
*Binds:* the order. *Drafting default:* batch boundaries may shift if
a screen finds a hand-off defect. *Evidence:* the last three days ran
three screen rounds per definition; batching by hand-off cuts that to
one screen per batch without losing the fresh-context check.
*Default:* on silence, proceed in this order.

**3. Accept what is left out.** *What you approve:* the annex's
exclusions — `completed` and the reconcile side, the changelog and
roadmap renderings, the `router` role, discovery forms beyond three,
and shops' co-production modeled as a marked hypothesis while shops
are frozen. *Binds:* nothing is built for these in the five batches.
*Drafting default:* each is filed in the definition that needs it.
*Evidence:* none is on the path from discovery to assignment.
*Default:* on silence, accepted.

## Deferred

- Approval of the definitions already drafted (initiative and feature
  chains, scenario assignment, the PO guidelines, three typedef
  amendments) — batch A's screen re-reads them in context; approve
  them with batch A rather than separately.

## Annex

[annex-032.md](annex-032.md) — the flow diagram, the sub-process table,
the build order, and the exclusions (optional, but the model is there).

## Document History

| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |

## Verdict: findings

## Stumbles in reading order (quotes)

1. Opening, "The gap you see is real: discovery ends at a session record" — "session record" arrives as a known thing; the reader knows discovery ends somewhere, not that its output is called a session record. Minor.
2. Opening, "composed of six sub-processes — three exist (discovery, the PO output check, scenario assignment)" — "the PO output check" is new naming; the reader cannot tell which existing process this is or whether it is the same thing as "the existing check" in Ask 1.
3. Opening, "Building it is five batches, four screens, five approvals as blocks" — five batches but four screens: the mismatch is unexplained and the reader stops to reconcile it. Ask 2 then says "each screened once as a set", which implies five screens. Contradiction inside the brief.
4. Opening, "about five sessions at the current pace" — "session" as a unit of work pace is not introduced; the reader has no calibration for it (a day? an hour?).
5. Ask 1, "discovery (brainstorm first) records an initiative as `proposed`" — "brainstorm first" is an aside that presupposes a set of discovery forms the reader has not been shown; Ask 3 later mentions "discovery forms beyond three" which confirms there is a taxonomy the brief never states.

7. Ask 1, "(`planned`, stays `proposed`, or `cancelled`)" — the state vocabulary appears without saying it is the initiative's state set; readable but heavy for one sentence, which runs seven clauses.
8. Ask 1, Evidence: "every hop the system read found undefined is now a named step" — "the system read" is unintroduced (it also appears in Document History as "the system read's judgment"). The reader does not know what read this was, when, or that it produced findings, so the evidence has no anchor. "which removes one pending process amendment" — which amendment, to which process, is not stated; the reader cannot weigh it.
9. Ask 2, "*Binds:* the order. *Drafting default:* batch boundaries may shift if a screen finds a hand-off defect." — a drafting default that can move batch boundaries partly unbinds the order the ask says is bound; the reader cannot tell what is fixed.
10. Ask 2, Evidence: "the last three days ran three screen rounds per definition" — number present, but "per definition" over how many definitions is not given, so the reader cannot size the saving; also "without losing the fresh-context check" asserts the property the reader would most want argued.
11. Ask 3, "`completed` and the reconcile side, the changelog and roadmap renderings, the `router` role" — every item is a bare identifier; "the reconcile side" is the hardest, as "reconcile" has not appeared before. The reader is asked to accept exclusions they cannot picture.
12. Ask 3, "shops' co-production modeled as a marked hypothesis while shops are frozen" — this item is different in kind from the others: it is included in the model (as a hypothesis) rather than excluded, yet it sits in the exclusion list. Then "*Binds:* nothing is built for these in the five batches" — but Ask 1 says the PO "authors each feature with the owning shops", which is the co-production; the reader cannot tell whether feature-authoring in batch scope depends on the thing being excluded.
13. Deferred, "Approval of the definitions already drafted (initiative and feature chains, scenario assignment, the PO guidelines, three typedef amendments) — ... approve them with batch A rather than separately." — this is a deferral written as a commitment: it fixes how those approvals will happen (with batch A). The reader has not been told what batch A contains. Also "three typedef amendments" — which typedefs is not said.
14. Annex line, "(optional, but the model is there)" — undercuts the optional label; Ask 1 asks approval of "the flow in the annex", so the reader is told the model they are approving is not in the brief. See Scenario 1.

## Terms not introduced (first mention, no gloss, not evidently shop vocabulary)

- "session record"
- "the PO output check" / "the existing check" (are these one process? name it)
- "session" as a pace unit
- "brainstorm first" (implies discovery forms)
- "the bet"
- "the system read"
- "pending process amendment" (which)
- "batches A–E" (contents never summarized in the brief)
- "the reconcile side"
- "changelog and roadmap renderings"
- "`router` role"
- "marked hypothesis"
- "batch A" (in Deferred)

Backticked identifiers (`product-flow`, `initiative-check`, `feature-authoring`, `backlog-ordering`, `proposed`, `planned`, `cancelled`, `completed`) are readable as new names being coined, so not counted, except `completed` which appears only in the exclusion list with no state set stated.

## Per-ask decidability

**Ask 1 — approve the model.** Wobbly. Binds vs drafting default: stated ("Binds: the six sub-processes and their hand-offs. Drafting default: step wording, prompts, and caps."). Recommendation, evidence, default all present. Why wobbly: the reader is approving "the flow in the annex", but the brief's one-sentence rendering has six sub-processes named in the opening and only five recognizable in the Ask 1 walkthrough (discovery, initiative-check, backlog placement, feature authoring + check, assignment — where is `backlog-ordering` versus "places it in the backlog order"? probably the same, but not said). The evidence rests on "the system read", which is unanchored. The reader can approve the shape; they cannot confirm the six are the six.

**Ask 2 — build order and block approval.** Wobbly, leaning cannot-decide. Binds vs default: stated but self-undermining (bound order, movable boundaries). Recommendation, evidence, default present. The reader is asked to approve "batches A–E in the annex" and the brief never says what a batch contains, how many definitions, or the order — the one thing being bound. The five-batches/four-screens mismatch adds doubt. Decidable only as "yes to batching in principle".

**Ask 3 — accept what is left out.** Cannot decide. Recommendation (implicit), default present, binds stated. Evidence is one sentence ("none is on the path from discovery to assignment") for five heterogeneous items, one of which (`completed`) is the end state of the very flow being modeled, and one (shops' co-production) appears to be in Ask 1's flow. The reader cannot picture three of the five items.

Gating statement for the set: present — "Ask 1 gates the work; asks 2 and 3 default on silence." Pass.

Commitments outside asks: the Deferred note commits an approval route ("approve them with batch A"); guideline rule 4 says make it an ask or a marked drafting default.

## Overload verdict

Right-sized in length; overloaded in density. The opening paragraph carries eleven numbers and names in six sentences; Ask 1's second sentence is seven clauses. For this reader — who wants a model and a plan, not a re-review — defer: the state vocabulary (`proposed`/`planned`/`cancelled`) and the exclusion list detail to the annex, and replace with what the reader needs to decide Ask 2: a five-line list of batch contents.

## Budgets

- Decision layer (answer-first + Asks): 412 words against ~400. At the line.
- Whole brief (title through annex link, excluding frontmatter and history): 471 words; file total 521. Well under ~1,500. Room exists to add the batch list and glosses.

| Scenario | Result | Note |

| 1 — decidable without the annex | Fail | Ask 1 approves "the flow in the annex"; Ask 2 approves "batches A–E in the annex" with no batch contents in the brief; Ask 3 approves "the annex's exclusions". Annex line itself says "the model is there". |
| 2 — first paragraph answers | Pass | "Recommendation: approve the model, the build order, and block approval per batch." |
| 3 — no unintroduced terms | Fail | List above; "the bet", "the system read", "the reconcile side", "batches A–E" are the load-bearing ones. |
| 4 (Then) — each ask complete | Pass | All three carry recommendation, evidence, default (Ask 3's recommendation is implicit in "Accept"; acceptable). |
| 4 (And) — gating stated | Pass | Quoted above. |

## Top three changes

1. Put the model in the brief: one line per sub-process (six lines: name, input, output, who acts) so Ask 1 approves something on the page, and reconcile the count (six named vs. five walked through; five batches vs. four screens).
2. Put the build order in the brief: batches A–E as five lines with contents and which existing definitions each re-screens; state what "bound order" survives boundary shifts. Move the Deferred note's "approve with batch A" into Ask 2 as a stated drafting default.
3. Gloss or cut the unanchored evidence and exclusions: name "the system read" (what, when), name the pending amendment, gloss "the bet" as the initiative go/no-go, and for Ask 3 give each exclusion a half-line of what it is — or drop the co-production item from the exclusions since it appears inside Ask 1's flow.
